claims.source: Generally, the expression pattern of the gfp allele that tags both isoforms matches the expression pattern reported using an antibody directed against both LIN-29 isoforms (Figure 3B) (Bettinger et al., 1996; Euling et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies.

claims.claim: Neuronal expression of lin-29 is almost completely restricted to the male and this male-specific expression can be entirely ascribed to the a-isoform.
claims.source: However, we found that this neuronal expression is almost completely restricted to the male and this male-specific expression can be entirely ascribed to the a-isoform (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claims.claim: The male-specific neuronal expression of lin-29a is not observed in male-specific neurons but is entirely restricted to sex-shared neurons.
claims.source: The male-specific neuronal expression of lin-29a is not observed in male-specific neurons but is, interestingly, entirely restricted to sex-shared neurons (i.e. neurons that are generated in both sexes).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation of lin-29a expression pattern.

claims.claim: 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes express lin-29a.
claims.source: Specifically, 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes express lin-29a, including seven sensory neuron classes in the head and tail (AWA, ASG, ASJ, ASK, ADF, PHB, PLM), seven interneuron classes (AVA, RIA, AIM, AVG, RIF, PVC, PVN), a few head and tail motor neurons (SAB, PDA, PDB) and most of the sex-shared ventral nerve cord motor neurons (dorsal and ventral A, B and D-type and AS neurons).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation of lin-29a expression pattern.

claims.claim: Many LIN-29A expressing neurons are synaptically connected to one another.
claims.source: Many of these LIN-29A expressing neurons are synaptically connected to one another (White et al., 1986) and some of the synaptic connections are known to be sexually dimorphic (Jarrell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Some of the synaptic connections between LIN-29A expressing neurons are known to be sexually dimorphic.
claims.source: Many of these LIN-29A expressing neurons are synaptically connected to one another (White et al., 1986) and some of the synaptic connections are known to be sexually dimorphic (Jarrell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Expression of lin-29a in all these neurons in the male nervous system is precisely temporally controlled; it is first observed in the early L4 stage and persists throughout adulthood.
claims.source: Expression of lin-29a in all these neurons in the male nervous system is precisely temporally controlled; it is first observed in the early L4 stage and persists throughout adulthood (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The lin-29b isoform is expressed in three postembryonically generated touch neurons (AVM, PVM, PDE), where its expression is not temporally regulated.
claims.source: In addition to the male-specific neuronal expression of the lin-29a isoform, we also found that the lin-29b isoform is expressed in three postembryonically generated touch neurons (AVM, PVM, PDE), where its expression is not temporally regulated, that is, its expression is induced right after the neurons are born in the first two larval stages and expression is observed in both sexes (data not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: The late larval onset of expression of lin-29 in non-neuronal cells has been reported to be controlled by the heterochronic pathway.
claims.source: The late larval onset of expression of lin-29 in non-neuronal cells has been reported to be controlled by the heterochronic pathway (Bettinger et al., 1996; Moss et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In lin-41(lf) mutants lin-29a::gfp expression is observed prematurely including in the sex-shared neurons of the male.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that in lin-41(lf) mutants lin-29a::gfp expression is observed prematurely including in the sex-shared neurons of the male (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In let-7(lf) and lin-41(gf) mutants, lin-29a::gfp expression levels are significantly reduced compared to wild-type adult males.
claims.source: As expected, in let-7(lf) and lin-41(gf) mutants (both of which maintain expression of LIN-41), lin-29a::gfp expression levels are significantly reduced compared to wild-type adult males (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: let-7-controlled LIN-41 directly represses lin-29a translation to control the precise timing of LIN-29A protein accumulation in the nervous system.
claims.source: Together with our previous biochemical analysis (Aeschimann et al., 2017), we conclude that let-7-controlled LIN-41 directly represses lin-29a translation to control the precise timing of LIN-29A protein accumulation in the nervous system.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and previous biochemical analysis.

claims.claim: In both lin-29a-isoform specific alleles (xe38 and xe40) the male-specific AIM neurotransmitter switch failed to occur.
claims.source: To assess the functional relevance of the lin-29a isoform in controlling the AIM neurotransmitter switch, we generated two lin-29a-isoform specific alleles (xe38 and xe40) using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering (Figure 3A) (Aeschimann et al., 2018). We indeed find that in both isoform-specific alleles the male-specific AIM neurotransmitter switch failed to occur (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: AIM-specific LIN-29A expression rescues the loss of the AIM neurotransmitter switch in adult male animals, thereby demonstrating cell autonomy of LIN-29A function.
claims.source: We found that in adult male animals, the loss of the AIM neurotransmitter switch (as assayed by cho-1 and unc-17 induction and eat-4 downregulation in AIM) is rescued by the transgene, thereby demonstrating cell autonomy of LIN-29A function (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The neurotransmitter switch is executed prematurely already by the first larval stage in transgenic animals ectopically expressing LIN-29A in AIM neurons.
claims.source: Examining juvenile males, before the onset of overt sexual maturation, we observed that the neurotransmitter switch is executed prematurely already by the first larval stage in these transgenic animals ectopically expressing LIN-29A in AIM neurons (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The temporal control of lin-29a expression, and specifically the repression of lin-29a by the heterochronic pathway is required to prevent lin-29a from triggering the neurotransmitter switch precociously.
claims.source: This sufficiency experiment indicates that the temporal control of lin-29a expression, and specifically the repression of lin-29a by the heterochronic pathway is required to prevent lin-29a from triggering the neurotransmitter switch precociously.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the sufficiency experiment showing premature neurotransmitter switch with ectopic lin-29a expression.

claims.claim: lin-29a is sufficient to induce the neurotransmitter switch in the opposite sex (hermaphrodites).
claims.source: Lastly, examining adult hermaphrodite animals expressing this construct, we found that lin-29a is sufficient to induce the neurotransmitter switch in the opposite sex (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: lin-29a is required and sufficient to control the AIM neurotransmitter switch.
claims.source: We conclude that lin-29a is required and sufficient to control the AIM neurotransmitter switch.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claims.claim: srj-54 fails to be expressed in lin-29a mutants.
claims.source: To assess whether lin-29a function in AIM goes beyond controlling AIM's neurotransmitter switch, we examined another molecular marker of sexually dimorphic AIM differentiation, the orphan GPCR, srj-54, which is induced in the AIM neurons upon male sexual differentiation (Portman, 2007). We found that srj-54 fails to be expressed in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6A) adding another AIM male-specific molecular feature that fails to be normally induced in the absence of lin-29.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: lin-29a mutants are defective in an AIM-mediated sexual behavioral paradigm.
claims.source: As we will describe further below, lin-29a mutants are also defective in an AIM-mediated sexual behavioral paradigm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data described later in the manuscript.

claims.claim: lin-29a is required for dmd-5 expression in AVG in males.
claims.source: First, the dmd-5 transcription factor was reported to be expressed in AVG neurons in adult males but not in hermaphrodites (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016). By analyzing the expression of a dmd-5 reporter in wild type versus lin-29a mutants, we found that lin-29a is required for dmd-5 expression in AVG in males (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The daf-7 gene, encoding a neuroendocrine TGFβ-like signal, is turned on during sexual maturation in the sex-shared ASJ neurons only in males.
claims.source: Second, the daf-7 gene, encoding a neuroendocrine TGFβ-like signal, is turned on during sexual maturation in the sex-shared ASJ neurons only in males (Hilbert and Kim, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons is abrogated in lin-29a mutants.
claims.source: This induction is also abrogated in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Non-sexually dimorphic expression of dmd-5 and daf-7 in other neuron types was not affected by lin-29a.
claims.source: Non-sexually dimorphic expression of dmd-5 and daf-7 in other neuron types was not affected by lin-29a.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation.

claims.claim: The lin-29a-expressing PDB motorneuron grows elaborate branches off from its cell body and initial segment of its posteriorly directed main process only in the male but not in the hermaphrodite.
claims.source: Specifically, the lin-29a-expressing PDB motorneuron located in the pre-anal ganglion grows elaborate branches off from its cell body and initial segment of its posteriorly directed main process. This was only observed in the male but not in the hermaphrodite (Jarrell et al., 2012; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Male-specific branches of PDB make extensive chemical and electrical synaptic contacts with both male-specific neurons, as well as sex-shared neurons.
claims.source: These male-specific branches make extensive chemical and electrical synaptic contacts with both male-specific neurons, as well as sex-shared neurons (Jarrell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Male-specific branches of PDB grow specifically during sexual maturation in the L4 stage.
claims.source: We corroborated the existence and reproducibility of male-specific branches by visualizing PDB with a reporter transgene (Figure 6C). We found that these branches grow specifically during sexual maturation in the L4 stage (Figure 6C), co-incident with the onset of lin-29a expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Growth of PDB branches is disrupted in lin-29a mutants.
claims.source: Growth of these branches is disrupted in lin-29a mutants (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: lin-29a affects multiple distinct types of sexual maturation events, from gene expression to anatomy, in distinct neuron classes.
claims.source: These findings demonstrate a role for lin-29a in regulating the temporal and sexually dimorphic acquisition of male-specific neuronal morphologies and predict that PDB fails to make its branch-specific synaptic contacts in the absence of lin-29a. We conclude that lin-29a affects multiple distinct types of sexual maturation events, from gene expression to anatomy, in distinct neuron classes.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in lin-29a mutants.

claims.claim: lin-29a mutant males do not display the obvious morphological and patterning defects displayed by the lin-29 null allele.
claims.source: Critical for such an analysis is the fact that lin-29a mutant males do not display the obvious morphological and patterning defects displayed by the lin-29 null allele.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation.

claims.claim: The male tail appears morphologically normal in lin-29a mutants.
claims.source: Specifically, the male tail, whose overall morphogenesis is disrupted in lin-29 null mutants (Euling et al., 1999) appears morphologically normal in lin-29a mutants (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: There are no overt morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males.
claims.source: We precisely quantified other morphological differences between hermaphrodites and males using an automated visualization/measurement tool (Yemini et al., 2013) and found no overt morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: lin-29a isoform-specific mutants were unable to mate.
claims.source: In spite of spicule patterning appearing normal in lin-29a isoform-specific mutants, we observed that these mutants were unable to mate (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: One aspect of mating behavior defective in lin-29a mutants is vulva location behavior.
claims.source: We found that one aspect of mating behavior defective in these mutants is vulva location behavior (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The AIM and ASJ neurons were previously implicated in mate-searching.
claims.source: The AIM and ASJ neurons, both of which express lin-29a specifically in males, were previously implicated in mate-searching, which constitutes another aspect of mating behavior (Barrios et al., 2012; Hilbert and Kim, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: lin-29a mutants are defective in mate searching behavior.
claims.source: We indeed found that lin-29a mutants are defective in mate searching behavior (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The mate searching defects of lin-29a mutants are similar to the defects caused by loss of daf-7/TGFβ.
claims.source: These defects are similar to the defects caused by loss of daf-7/TGFβ (Hilbert and Kim, 2017) and, consistent with this phenotypic similarity, we had described above that daf-7/TGFβ expression is lost in the ASJ neurons of lin-29a mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies and experimental data.

claims.claim: The mate searching defects of the lin-29a mutant males can be partially rescued by restoring LIN-29A expression exclusively in the AIM neurons.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we could partially rescue the mate searching defects of the lin-29a mutant males by restoring LIN-29A expression exclusively in the AIM neurons (Figure 7D), indicating that lin-29a may function in several distinct neurons to control mate searching behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Adult male and hermaphrodites display distinct locomotor behavior when crawling on a lawn of bacteria.
claims.source: The male-specific expression of lin-29a in ventral nerve cord and head motor neurons and in a command interneuron pair made us consider whether lin-29a may be involved in controlling aspects of sexually dimorphic locomotor behavior. It has previously been shown that adult male and hermaphrodites display distinct locomotor behavior when crawling on a lawn of bacteria (Mowrey et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: lin-29a mutants displayed a striking feminization of a number of body posture and locomotory features.
claims.source: We found a large number of sexually dimorphic features. While many of them were not affected in lin-29a mutant animals (Figure 8 and Supplementary file 1), we found that lin-29a mutants displayed a striking feminization of a number of body posture and locomotory features.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The lack of morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males indicates that locomotory phenotypes are the result of neuronal defects rather than being a secondary consequence of overall body morphology.
claims.source: The lack of morphological differences between wild-type and lin-29a mutant males indicates that these locomotory phenotypes are the result of neuronal defects rather than being a secondary consequence of overall body morphology.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that morphology is normal but behavior is affected.

claims.claim: lin-29a is required for the acquisition of male-specific postural and locomotory features.
claims.source: Taken together, these results show that lin-29a is required for the acquisition of male-specific postural and locomotory features and that the absence of lin-29a results in a feminization of these behavioral parameters.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the feminization of behavioral features in lin-29a mutants.

claims.claim: Expression of lin-29a in the motor circuit, using a cis-regulatory element from the unc-17/VAChT locus rescued a defined subset of the feminized behavioral features (wavelength, crawling amplitude and midbody bend).
claims.source: We sought to determine in which of the neurons that express lin-29a in a sexually dimorphic manner lin-29a acts to control aspects of the locomotor behaviors described above. We particularly considered the so-called 'motor circuit', composed of a set of command interneurons and ventral nerve cord motor neurons (Von Stetina et al., 2006). Expression of lin-29a in the motor circuit, using a cis-regulatory element from the unc-17/VAChT locus rescued a defined subset of the feminized behavioral features (wavelength, crawling amplitude and midbody bend) (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: In tra-1(e1488) mutants, lin-29a expression becomes derepressed in XX animals.
claims.source: To assess the control of sex-specificity of lin-29a expression, we genetically removed tra-1, the master regulatory transcription factor of sex determination which is normally expressed in all hermaphroditic cells (XX sex chromosome genotype) where it suppresses male identities (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006). We found that in tra-1(e1488) mutants, lin-29a expression becomes derepressed in XX animals (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Degradation of tra-1 exclusively in the nervous system by force-expressing fem-3 under the control of a panneuronal driver derepresses lin-29a expression in the nervous system of the hermaphrodite, with the same pattern of cellular specificity seen normally in males.
claims.source: Moreover, we induced the degradation of tra-1 exclusively in the nervous system by force-expressing fem-3, which promotes TRA-1 protein destruction (Starostina et al., 2007), under the control of a panneuronal driver. We found that lin-29a expression is derepressed in the nervous system of the hermaphrodite, with the same pattern of cellular specificity seen normally in males (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The POU homeobox transcription factor unc-86 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AIM interneurons.
claims.source: For example, the terminal differentiation program of the lin-29a expressing ASK neurons is controlled by the LIM homeobox gene ttx-3/LHX2 and the identity of the AIM neuron is defined by the unc-86/BRN3 POU homeobox gene (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013). We found that lin-29a expression is eliminated in the ASK neurons of ttx-3 mutants and in the AIM neurons of unc-86 mutants (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The LIM-HD transcription factor ttx-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in ASK.
claims.source: For example, the terminal differentiation program of the lin-29a expressing ASK neurons is controlled by the LIM homeobox gene ttx-3/LHX2 and the identity of the AIM neuron is defined by the unc-86/BRN3 POU homeobox gene (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013). We found that lin-29a expression is eliminated in the ASK neurons of ttx-3 mutants and in the AIM neurons of unc-86 mutants (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The COE/EBF transcription factor unc-3 is required for lin-29a/b::gfp expression in AVA, SAB, DA, DB, VA, VB, PDA, PDB and PVC neurons.
claims.source: The unc-3/COE-type transcription factor controls the identity of multiple neurons of the motor circuit, including the lin-29a expressing ventral nerve cord motorneurons, the SAB head motor neurons, the PDA and PDB tail motor neurons and the command interneurons AVA and PVC (Kratsios et al., 2011; Pereira et al., 2015). We found that in unc-3 mutants lin-29a expression is lost in all these neurons (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The complex lin-29a expression pattern can be explained by an intersectional mechanism where temporal control is exerted via the heterochronic pathway, sexual specificity by the sex determination pathway and cellular specificity by terminal selector-type neuronal identity factors.
claims.source: We conclude that the complex lin-29a expression pattern can be explained by an intersectional mechanism. Temporal control is exerted via the heterochronic pathway, sexual specificity by the sex determination pathway and cellular specificity by terminal selector-type neuronal identity factors.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the multiple regulatory inputs controlling lin-29a expression.

claims.claim: The sexually dimorphic expression pattern of lin-29a in the male nervous system does not extend to all sex-shared neurons that are known to display sexually dimorphic features.
claims.source: The sexually dimorphic expression pattern of lin-29a in the male nervous system does not extend to all sex-shared neurons that are known to display sexually dimorphic features.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation.

claims.claim: The sex-shared PHC sensory neuron functionally and anatomically remodels during sexual maturation but does not express lin-29a.
claims.source: For example, the sex-shared PHC sensory neuron functionally and anatomically remodels during sexual maturation (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a), but does not express lin-29a.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: LIN-41 also represses mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA.
claims.source: Previous whole animal RNA profiling of let-7 and lin-41 mutants, as well as RNA-binding assays demonstrated that LIN-41 also represses mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA (Aeschimann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: mab-3 and dmd-3 are members of the DMD family of sex-specifically expressed transcription factors.
claims.source: Both genes are members of the DMD family of sex-specifically expressed transcription factors (Mason et al., 2008; Yi and Zarkower, 1999) and were previously shown to be expressed in male-specific neurons and in a male-specific manner in distinct, but sex-shared neurons (Mason et al., 2008; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a; Yi et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Within the sex-shared nervous system, mab-3 is not only male-specifically expressed in the ADF neuron, but also in additional head neurons, including the embryonically generated SMD head motor neurons.
claims.source: We gfp-tagged the endogenous mab-3 and dmd-3 loci using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering. Within the sex-shared nervous system, we found that mab-3 is not only male-specifically expressed in the ADF neuron, as previously reported (Yi et al., 2000), but also in additional head neurons, including the embryonically generated SMD head motor neurons (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: Male-specific neuronal expression of mab-3 is precisely timed to commence at the L4 stage.
claims.source: We found that like the male-specific, neuronal expression of lin-29a, male-specific neuronal expression of mab-3 is precisely timed to commence at the L4 stage (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: The gfp-tagged dmd-3 locus is expressed in a sex-shared neuron class, the PHC neurons.
claims.source: Similarly, the gfp-tagged dmd-3 locus is expressed in a sex-shared neuron class, the PHC neurons (Figure 9D), where dmd-3 acts to control the sexually dimorphic remodeling of PHC (Mason et al., 2008; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: dmd-3::gfp expression in PHC commences at the L4 stage.
claims.source: dmd-3::gfp expression in PHC also commences at the L4 stage (Figure 9D), at the time when PHC neurons remodel in a male-specific manner (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: The temporal specificity of nervous system expression of mab-3 and dmd-3 is lost in let-7 mutants.
claims.source: We corroborated our previous data of LIN-41 protein affecting mab-3 and dmd-3 expression (Aeschimann et al., 2017) by showing that the temporal specificity of nervous system expression of mab-3 and dmd-3 is indeed lost in let-7 mutants (Figure 9C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C-D.

claims.claim: The male-specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in the nervous system is controlled by the tra-1 transcription factor.
claims.source: Like lin-29a, the male-specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression in the nervous system is controlled by the tra-1 transcription factor (Figure 9E,G)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E,G (note: Figure 9G is referenced but should be 9F based on the figure labels).

claims.claim: The neuronal specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression is controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selectors.
claims.source: Moreover, the neuronal specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 expression is, like lin-29a, also controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selectors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing terminal selector requirements.

claims.claim: unc-42 is a terminal selector transcription factor that controls terminal differentiation of the RMD and SMD neurons.
claims.source: unc-42 is a terminal selector transcription factor that controls terminal differentiation of the RMD and SMD neurons (Pereira et al., 2015), and we found that mab-3 expression in these neurons fails to be induced in an unc-42 mutant background (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: mab-3 expression in RMD and SMD neurons fails to be induced in an unc-42 mutant background.
claims.source: unc-42 is a terminal selector transcription factor that controls terminal differentiation of the RMD and SMD neurons (Pereira et al., 2015), and we found that mab-3 expression in these neurons fails to be induced in an unc-42 mutant background (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: ceh-14 is a terminal selector of PHC neuron identity.
claims.source: Similarly, ceh-14 is a terminal selector of PHC neuron identity (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a) and is required for dmd-3 expression in PHC (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: ceh-14 is required for dmd-3 expression in PHC.
claims.source: Similarly, ceh-14 is a terminal selector of PHC neuron identity (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2017a) and is required for dmd-3 expression in PHC (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: lin-41 operates through multiple distinct, male-specific effector genes and the temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of expression of these distinct effectors is controlled by a similar, intersectional regulatory logic.
claims.source: We conclude that lin-41 operates through multiple distinct, male-specific effector genes and that the temporal, sexual and spatial specificity of expression of these distinct effectors is controlled by a similar, intersectional regulatory logic (Figure 10A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar regulatory patterns observed for lin-29a, mab-3, and dmd-3.

claims.claim: The conservation of the deployment of the lin-28/let-7 pathway in the timing of sexual maturation is remarkable.
claims.source: We have described here that the timing of multiple distinct, neuron-type specific sexually dimorphic maturation events in the nervous system of C. elegans are controlled by a phylogenetically conserved regulatory cassette composed of ubiquitously expressed and temporally controlled genes, lin-28 (a regulator of let-7 miRNA processing), let-7 (a miRNA) and its target lin-41 (a translational regulator). The conservation of the deployment of this pathway in the timing of sexual maturation is remarkable.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison with findings in other organisms.

claims.claim: Genetic manipulations in mice, as well as genome-wide association studies of humans with abnormally timed puberty demonstrate that lin-28 and let-7 also control timing of sexual maturation (puberty) onset in mammals.
claims.source: Genetic manipulations in mice, as well as genome-wide association studies of humans with abnormally timed puberty demonstrate that lin-28 and let-7 also control timing of sexual maturation (puberty) onset in mammals (Chen et al., 2017; Corre et al., 2016; He et al., 2009; Ong et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2009; Sulem et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mutations in human makorin, the orthologue of lep-2, a regulator of lin-28 activity in C. elegans, also affect the timing of puberty in humans.
claims.source: This conclusion was further corroborated by the finding that mutations in human makorin, the orthologue of lep-2, a regulator of lin-28 activity in C. elegans (Herrera et al., 2016), also affect the timing of puberty in humans (Abreu et al., 2013; Bulcao Macedo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In the fly nervous system, lin-28 and let-7 are involved in controlling the timing of pupal to adult transitions.
claims.source: Similarly, in the fly nervous system, lin-28 and let-7 are involved in controlling the timing of pupal to adult transitions (González-Itier et al., 2018; Sempere et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2012) that are accompanied by sexual maturation in the nervous system, as assessed by expression of the male-specific isoform of Fruitless, a master regulator of male-specific nervous system differentiation (Lee et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A regulatory linkage between the heterochronic pathway and transcriptional regulators of sexual differentiation (hormone receptors in vertebrates or Fruitless in flies) has not yet been established in vertebrates or flies.
claims.source: However, a regulatory linkage between the heterochronic pathway and transcriptional regulators of sexual differentiation (hormone receptors in vertebrates or Fruitless in flies) has not yet been established in these systems.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reported findings in the literature.

claims.source: The let-7 miRNA is known to have a plethora of distinct mRNA targets (Büssing et al., 2008), but the one that we define here as being relevant in the context of sexual maturation is the translational regulator lin-41 (Slack et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: C. elegans lin-41 had previously been implicated as an output of let-7 in the timing of skin cell maturation events.
claims.source: C. elegans lin-41 had previously been implicated as an output of let-7 in the timing of skin cell maturation events (Slack et al., 2000) as well as vulval patterning (Ecsedi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: lin-41 is highly conserved in vertebrates where its expression appears to be temporally regulated during embryogenesis with its expression being complementary to let-7.
claims.source: lin-41 is also highly conserved in vertebrates where its expression appears to be temporally regulated during embryogenesis with its expression being complementary to let-7, as observed in C. elegans (Schulman et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The dynamics of lin-28, let-7 and lin-41 expression has not yet been comprehensively examined in the context of sexual maturation in the vertebrate brain.
claims.source: The dynamics of lin-28, let-7 and lin-41 expression has not yet been comprehensively examined in the context of sexual maturation in the vertebrate brain, but notably, the expression of Lin28 and Let7 in the hypothalamus, a site of release of peptides that control pubertal onset, appears to be temporally controlled (Sangiao-Alvarellos et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of comprehensive studies and a citation to a limited study.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, let-7 expression has been found to be temporally regulated; its expression increases during late pupal stages.
claims.source: In Drosophila, let-7 expression has also been found to be temporally regulated; its expression increases during late pupal stages (Faunes and Larraín, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: A role of Drosophila let-7 in the timing of sexual maturation has not yet been assessed.
claims.source: This is the time at which at least some parts of the Drosophila nervous system sexually mature (Lee et al., 2000), but a role of Drosophila let-7 in the timing of sexual maturation has not yet been assessed.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reported findings in the literature.

claims.claim: A previously described upstream regulator of lin-28, the lin-4 miRNA, does not affect male-specific sexual maturation in the nervous system.
claims.source: One key remaining question, raised by our studies in C. elegans, is how lin-28/Lin28 function is precisely timed in the nervous system. Surprisingly, we found that a previously described upstream regulator of lin-28, the lin-4 miRNA (Moss et al., 1997), does not affect male-specific sexual maturation in the nervous system, suggesting the existence of alternative pathways that determine when lin-28's function in controlling let-7 processing is downregulated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: Recent work in C. elegans has discovered LIN-28 protein degradation, mediated by the conserved LEP-2/Makorin protein, as another means to control lin-28 function.
claims.source: Recent work in C. elegans has discovered LIN-28 protein degradation, mediated by the conserved LEP-2/Makorin protein, as another means to control lin-28 function (Herrera et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The key target of let-7, the lin-41 translational regulator, relays temporal information in a modular manner to distinct, neuron class-specific outputs.
claims.source: We showed here that the key target of let-7, the lin-41 translational regulator, relays temporal information in a modular manner to distinct, neuron class-specific outputs (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing distinct effectors in different neuron types.

claims.claim: The vertebrate orthologs of LIN-29, ZNF362 and ZNF384, are completely unstudied.
claims.source: Among them is the phylogenetically conserved LIN-29 Zn finger transcription factor (whose vertebrate orthologs ZNF362 and ZNF384 are completely unstudied), which we identified as being sexually dimorphically expressed in one fifth of all sex-shared neuron classes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reported studies on these proteins.

claims.claim: Two other targets of lin-41 that are relevant for sexual maturation are two male-specifically expressed DM domain transcription factors.
claims.source: Two other targets of lin-41 that are relevant for sexual maturation are two male-specifically expressed DM domain transcription factors (Aeschimann et al., 2017) (this paper).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in this paper and a previous study.

claims.claim: Neurons that express sexually dimorphic output regulators (lin-29, mab-3, dmd-3) act at distinct levels of information processing, from sensory, to inter- to motorneurons.
claims.source: Neurons that express these sexually dimorphic output regulators (lin-29, mab-3, dmd-3) act at distinct levels of information processing, from sensory, to inter- to motorneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the known functions of the neurons expressing these regulators.

claims.claim: Many of the sex-shared, LIN-29(+) interneurons are synaptically connected and some of these connections are sexually dimorphic.
claims.source: Intriguingly, many of the sex-shared, LIN-29(+) interneurons are synaptically connected and some of these connections are sexually dimorphic.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on known connectivity data.

claims.claim: Some of the neurons that express LIN-29 or MAB-3 in a male-specific manner were not previously shown to display any sexual dimorphisms.
claims.source: Some of the neurons that express LIN-29 or MAB-3 in a male-specific manner were not previously shown to display any sexual dimorphisms, demonstrating that the C. elegans nervous system may be even more sexually dimorphic than previously appreciated.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the novel expression patterns observed.

claims.claim: lin-29, mab-3 and dmd-3 expression mark many, but not quite all sex-shared neurons with sexually dimorphic features.
claims.source: lin-29, mab-3 and dmd-3 expression mark many, but not quite all sex-shared neurons with sexually dimorphic features.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation.

claims.claim: A ubiquitously expressed temporal coordinate system (heterochronic pathway), intersects with a ubiquitously expressed sexual coordinate system (sex determination pathway) to control the sexual and temporal specificity of a number of modular, neuron-type specific output systems that control sexual dimorphisms in distinct cellular circuit modules.
claims.source: Altogether, these findings suggest a scenario in which a ubiquitously expressed temporal coordinate system (heterochronic pathway), intersects with a ubiquitously expressed sexual coordinate system (sex determination pathway) to control the sexual and temporal specificity of a number of modular, neuron-type specific output systems that control sexual dimorphisms in distinct cellular circuit modules (Figure 10A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing intersectional control.

claims.claim: This modular organization displays striking conceptual similarities with the modular organization of sexual dimorphic control mechanisms in vertebrates.
claims.source: This modular organization displays striking conceptual similarities with the modular organization of sexual dimorphic control mechanisms in vertebrates (Yang and Shah, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison with vertebrate systems and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The neuron-type specificity of the modular outputs (lin-29, mab-3, dmd-3 etc.) of the temporal and sex-determination system is controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selector transcription factors which define the overall differentiated state of individual neuron classes.
claims.source: We provided evidence here that the neuron-type specificity of the sex-specific regulator is controlled by neuron-type specific terminal selector transcription factors which define the overall differentiated state of individual neuron classes (Hobert, 2016) (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing terminal selector requirements.

claims.claim: The regulation of lin-29 by the temporal cue lin-41 could potentially be direct since several phylogenetically conserved binding sites for UNC-3 protein were noted in the lin-29 locus.
claims.source: Like the regulation of lin-29 by the temporal cue lin-41, the neuron-type specific regulation of lin-29 could potentially be direct since we noted several phylogenetically conserved binding sites for UNC-3 protein in the lin-29 locus.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative based on the presence of conserved binding sites.

claims.claim: In the male AIM neurons, unc-86 and ceh-14 are required for the induction of unc-17 and cho-1 expression.
claims.source: The regulation of sex-specific output regulators, like lin-29, by terminal selectors reveals the potential existence of a specific gene regulatory network architecture. For example, in the male AIM neurons, unc-86 and ceh-14 are required for the induction of unc-17 and cho-1 expression (Pereira et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: unc-86 and ceh-14 are apparently not sufficient to induce unc-17 and cho-1 expression in hermaphrodites, but via the unc-86-mediated induction of lin-29 expression in the AIM neurons in males, unc-86 and ceh-14 are now apparently able to induce, with the help of lin-29, the expression of unc-17 and cho-1.
claims.source: Both are apparently not sufficient to induce unc-17 and cho-1 expression in hermaphrodites, but via the unc-86-mediated induction of lin-29 expression in the AIM neurons in males, unc-86 and ceh-14 are now apparently able to induce, with the help of lin-29, the expression of unc-17 and cho-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the regulatory relationships observed.

results.result: The heterochronic pathway genes lin-28, let-7, and lin-41 control the timing of sexually dimorphic neuronal differentiation in C. elegans males. Loss-of-function mutations in lin-28 and lin-41 cause precocious differentiation of AIM and CEM neurons, while loss of let-7 or gain-of-function lin-41 blocks male-specific differentiation.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent genetic manipulations (C22-C27, C31-C34, C38-C42, C45-C48) consistently demonstrate temporal control by the heterochronic pathway. The opposing phenotypes of loss-of-function versus gain-of-function alleles provide strong genetic evidence. Quantification in Figure 1D,F supports the claims with n=15 for each genotype. The precocious phenotypes in lin-28 and lin-41(lf) mutants and blocked differentiation in let-7(lf) and lin-41(gf) mutants are internally consistent with the proposed regulatory hierarchy.

results.result: The timing of male-specific neuronal differentiation is independent of gonadal signals and the lin-4 miRNA. Neither germline removal nor gonad ablation affects the AIM neurotransmitter switch, and lin-4 mutants show normal timing of differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C36 and C37 are supported by both genetic (glp-1 mutants) and physical ablation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The negative results for lin-4 (C37, C49, C146) are important controls that distinguish L4-specific timing from earlier L2-specific heterochronic events. However, the manuscript notes these are unpublished observations ('data not shown'), which slightly weakens reproducibility assessment.

results.result: The lin-29 transcription factor is the relevant effector of lin-41 in controlling the AIM neurotransmitter switch but not CEM differentiation. Lin-29 null mutants and lin-29a-specific mutants completely block the AIM neurotransmitter switch while CEM differentiation remains unaffected.
results.evaluation: The differential requirement for lin-29 in AIM versus CEM neurons (C53-C54) is well-supported by loss-of-function analysis in Figure 1C-F. The generation of two independent lin-29a-specific alleles (xe38 and xe40) that phenocopy the null allele (C82) provides strong genetic evidence. The cell-type-specific effects (C55) demonstrate that lin-41 acts through distinct effectors in different neurons, which is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: The transcriptional co-factor mab-10 is not required for lin-29 function in male-specific neuronal differentiation, despite being a direct target of LIN-41 and functioning with lin-29 in epidermal differentiation.
results.evaluation: The newly generated mab-10 null allele (xe44) shows normal AIM and CEM differentiation (C59, Figure 1D,F), demonstrating tissue-specific cofactor requirements. This negative result is important for defining the specificity of the pathway. However, the manuscript notes in the Methods that the mab-10::mCherry allele is not fully functional, which raises questions about whether xe44 is a true null or whether there might be redundancy.

results.result: The heterochronic pathway components show temporally controlled, sexually non-dimorphic expression in the nervous system. lin-28 is downregulated by L2, lin-41 is downregulated at L4 in a let-7-dependent manner, and let-7 activity increases at L4.
results.evaluation: Expression analysis using fosmid reporters (C62), endogenously tagged alleles (C63), and let-7 activity sensors (C65-C66) provides multiple lines of evidence for temporal control. The control construct with unc-54 3'UTR (C66) is an appropriate negative control. The lack of sexual dimorphism in expression (C68) is important for establishing that temporal and sexual specificity arise at the level of downstream effectors rather than pathway components.

results.result: The lin-29a isoform is expressed in a male-specific, temporally controlled manner in 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes, with expression initiating at L4 and persisting through adulthood. Expression is restricted to sex-shared neurons, not male-specific neurons.
results.evaluation: Multiple CRISPR-engineered reporter alleles (gfp::lin-29a, lin-29a/b::gfp, lin-29b::gfp) provide comprehensive expression analysis (C69-C73, Figure 3). The specificity to sex-shared neurons (C72) is a surprising and important finding. The temporal onset at L4 (C76) correlates with the timing of sexual differentiation. The detailed neuronal identification across 21 neuron classes (C73) represents substantial characterization work.

results.result: LIN-41 directly represses lin-29a translation to control the timing of LIN-29A protein accumulation in the nervous system. lin-41 loss-of-function causes premature lin-29a expression, while let-7 loss-of-function and lin-41 gain-of-function reduce lin-29a expression.
results.evaluation: The genetic epistasis experiments (C79-C80, Figure 4) are consistent with direct translational repression. The claim of direct repression (C81) is supported by citing previous biochemical analysis (Aeschimann et al., 2017), which strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. The opposing effects of lin-41(lf) versus lin-41(gf) on lin-29a expression provide strong genetic evidence for regulation.

results.result: lin-29a is necessary and sufficient to control the AIM neurotransmitter switch. Cell-autonomous expression of lin-29a rescues the switch in mutants, induces it prematurely in juveniles, and can impose male-specific features in hermaphrodites.
results.evaluation: The sufficiency experiments using AIM-specific expression (C83-C86, Figure 5B) are well-designed and demonstrate three key points: cell autonomy, temporal sufficiency, and sex-specificity override. The use of two independent transgenic lines for each construct strengthens the conclusions. The premature induction in L1 larvae (C84) and sex conversion in hermaphrodites (C86) are particularly compelling demonstrations of sufficiency.

results.result: lin-29a controls multiple aspects of male-specific neuronal differentiation beyond the AIM neurotransmitter switch, including expression of srj-54 in AIM, dmd-5 in AVG, daf-7 in ASJ, and male-specific branching of PDB neurons.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent molecular markers (C88, C90, C92) and morphological features (C96-C97) demonstrate broad roles for lin-29a. The specificity of effects (C93) - non-sexually dimorphic expression unaffected - is an important control. The PDB branching phenotype (Figure 6C) provides quantitative morphological data (n=10). These diverse phenotypes establish lin-29a as a master regulator rather than a gene-specific factor.

results.result: lin-29a mutant males show normal overall morphology and body patterning, unlike lin-29 null mutants. The male tail appears normal and automated morphometric analysis reveals no significant differences from wild-type males.
results.evaluation: The distinction between lin-29a-specific and lin-29 null phenotypes (C99-C100) is important for interpreting behavioral defects. The automated WormTracker analysis (C101, Figure 7B) provides objective, quantitative morphological measurements. This establishes that behavioral phenotypes are due to neuronal defects rather than gross morphological abnormalities, strengthening the neurobiological interpretation.

results.result: lin-29a mutant males are defective in mating behaviors including vulva location and mate searching. The mate searching defects can be partially rescued by restoring lin-29a expression specifically in AIM neurons.
results.evaluation: The behavioral assays (C102-C103, C105, Figure 7C-D) demonstrate functional consequences of lin-29a loss. The partial rescue by AIM-specific expression (C107) provides evidence for cell-autonomous function and suggests multiple neurons contribute to the behavior. The similarity to daf-7 mutant phenotypes (C106) is consistent with the loss of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons. Sample sizes (n=15) are adequate for behavioral assays.

results.result: lin-29a mutant males show feminization of specific locomotory and postural features including head bend, neck bend, midbody bend, wavelength, and crawling amplitude. Restoring lin-29a expression in the motor circuit partially rescues some feminized features.
results.evaluation: The automated WormTracker analysis (C109, Figure 8) provides objective, high-dimensional behavioral phenotyping with n=20 animals. The specificity of effects - many sexually dimorphic features are unaffected - demonstrates that lin-29a controls a subset of dimorphic behaviors. The inference that phenotypes result from neuronal defects (C110) is well-supported by the lack of morphological differences. The partial rescue by motor circuit expression (C112) provides anatomical localization.

results.result: The sex-specificity of lin-29a expression is controlled by the sex determination pathway through TRA-1. Removal of tra-1 or nervous system-specific degradation of TRA-1 derepresses lin-29a expression in hermaphrodites with male-typical cellular specificity.
results.evaluation: The tra-1 mutant analysis (C113) and tissue-specific masculinization experiments (C114, Figure 9A) provide strong evidence for sex-determination pathway control. The maintenance of cellular specificity in masculinized hermaphrodites (C114) demonstrates that sex-specificity and neuron-type specificity are independently controlled. The intersectional model (C118) integrates temporal, sexual, and spatial control mechanisms.

results.result: The neuron-type specificity of lin-29a expression is controlled by terminal selector transcription factors. unc-86 is required for expression in AIM, ttx-3 for ASK, and unc-3 for motor circuit neurons including ventral nerve cord motor neurons and command interneurons.
results.evaluation: The terminal selector mutant analysis (C115-C117, Figure 9B) demonstrates cell-type-specific control. The use of multiple terminal selectors controlling different subsets of lin-29a-expressing neurons (C157) provides strong evidence for the intersectional model. This explains how a single gene can be expressed in diverse neuron types - each requires its own terminal selector plus temporal and sexual inputs.

results.result: LIN-41 also represses mab-3 and dmd-3, two DM domain transcription factors that show male-specific, temporally controlled expression in distinct sex-shared neurons. These genes are regulated by similar intersectional mechanisms involving let-7, tra-1, and neuron-specific terminal selectors.
results.evaluation: The CRISPR-tagged mab-3 and dmd-3 alleles (C123, C125) reveal novel expression patterns and L4-specific onset (C124, C126). The loss of temporal specificity in let-7 mutants (C127) and sex-specificity control by tra-1 (C128) parallel lin-29a regulation. Terminal selector requirements (C129, C131, C133) complete the intersectional model. This demonstrates that the regulatory logic extends beyond lin-29a to other effectors.

results.result: LIN-29 is an ortholog of human ZNF362 and ZNF384 based on sequence homology of zinc finger domains.
results.evaluation: The sequence alignment (C21, Figure 1A) shows conservation of zinc finger domains and DNA-contacting residues. The manuscript notes using multiple orthology tools (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017) and detailed analysis of DNA binding features. However, functional orthology would require additional evidence beyond sequence similarity. The claim is appropriately limited to sequence-based orthology.

results.result: The lin-28/let-7 pathway's role in controlling timing of sexual maturation is phylogenetically conserved. Studies in mice and humans link lin-28 and let-7 to puberty timing, mutations in human makorin (lep-2 ortholog) affect puberty, and Drosophila lin-28/let-7 control pupal-to-adult transitions.
results.evaluation: The conservation claims (C135-C138) are well-supported by multiple citations to published studies in mammals and flies. This contextualizes the C. elegans findings within a broader evolutionary framework. However, the manuscript appropriately notes (C139) that direct regulatory linkage to sexual differentiation transcription factors has not been established in vertebrates or flies, identifying an important gap.

results.result: Sexual dimorphisms in the C. elegans nervous system include sex-specific neurons and sexually dimorphic features of sex-shared neurons. Most sexually dimorphic features differentiate during the fourth larval stage.
results.evaluation: These background claims (C6-C14) are well-supported by citations to established literature. They provide essential context for the current work. The timing of differentiation at L4 (C14) is particularly important as it motivated the investigation of L4-specific heterochronic genes. These are appropriately cited prior work rather than novel findings.

results.result: Heterochronic genes control the timing of developmental events in C. elegans. The pathway includes lin-28, let-7, and lin-41, with LIN-28 negatively regulating let-7 processing and LIN-41 being a key let-7 target. Their role in postmitotic cells is less well defined than in controlling cell division patterns.
results.evaluation: These claims (C15-C20) summarize well-established prior work on the heterochronic pathway, appropriately cited. The acknowledgment that roles in postmitotic cells are less well defined (C20) motivates the current investigation. This represents accurate representation of the field's knowledge state.

results.result: Background on CEM neurons, lin-41 function, lin-29 regulation, and mab-10 function based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: These claims (C43-C44, C50-C52, C56-C58, C60) accurately represent prior published work. They provide necessary background for interpreting the current findings. The citations are appropriate and the claims are consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: Background information on neuronal connectivity, gene expression patterns, and transcription factor functions from prior literature.
results.evaluation: These claims cite established findings about synaptic connectivity (C74-C75), gene expression (C91), neuronal morphology (C94-C95), behavior (C104, C108), and transcription factors (C130, C132). The citations are appropriate and provide context for the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of gaps in knowledge and conservation of pathway components across species, including absence of established regulatory linkages in vertebrates/flies, multiple let-7 targets, conservation of lin-41, and limited studies in vertebrate brain.
results.evaluation: These claims (C139-C145, C147, C149) appropriately identify gaps in the field and areas for future investigation. They are based on absence of published findings (knowledge-based evidence) or limited studies. The acknowledgment of what is not known is important for contextualizing the significance of the current work.

results.result: Synthesis and interpretation: lin-41 relays temporal information to distinct neuron-specific outputs including lin-29a and DM domain transcription factors. These effectors act in neurons at different levels of information processing, and the modular organization shows conceptual similarities to vertebrate sexual dimorphism mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These synthetic claims (C148-C156) integrate the experimental findings into a coherent model. The modular organization concept (C155) is well-supported by the data showing distinct effectors in different neuron types. The comparison to vertebrate mechanisms (C156) is appropriately tentative ('conceptual similarities'). The identification of novel expression patterns (C153) and incomplete coverage (C154) appropriately acknowledge limitations.

results.result: Speculation about potential direct regulation and feedforward regulatory architecture based on presence of conserved binding sites and regulatory relationships.
results.evaluation: These claims (C158, C160) are explicitly speculative. C158 notes 'could potentially be direct' based on conserved UNC-3 binding sites, and C160 proposes a feedforward architecture that is inferred but not directly tested. The manuscript appropriately indicates these require 'further biochemical studies' for confirmation. These represent reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: lin-29a expression does not extend to all sex-shared neurons with sexually dimorphic features, such as PHC neurons which remodel during sexual maturation but do not express lin-29a.
results.evaluation: The observation that PHC neurons show sexual dimorphism without lin-29a expression (C119-C120) is important for defining the scope of lin-29a function. This motivates the investigation of other LIN-41 targets like dmd-3 that are expressed in PHC. The claim is supported by expression analysis and prior knowledge of PHC remodeling.

results.result: The heterochronic pathway genes lin-28, let-7, and lin-41 control the timing of the AIM neurotransmitter switch in C. elegans males. Loss-of-function mutations in lin-28 and lin-41 cause precocious differentiation, while loss-of-function mutations in let-7 or gain-of-function mutations in lin-41 block the switch.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers were 'very enthusiastic about the conceptual and technical aspects of the work and recommended acceptance.' No concerns were raised about the core findings regarding heterochronic pathway control of AIM differentiation timing. The only comments were minor figure presentation issues.

results.result: lin-29 is required for the AIM neurotransmitter switch but not for CEM neuron differentiation, indicating that lin-41 controls distinct effector genes in different neuron types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning these findings. The differential requirement for lin-29 in different neuron types is a key finding that was not challenged.

results.result: The heterochronic pathway genes also control the timing of CEM neuron differentiation. lin-28 and lin-41 loss-of-function mutants show precocious cholinergic gene expression, while let-7 and lin-41 gain-of-function mutants fail to express cholinergic genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers were enthusiastic about the work and recommended acceptance. No concerns were raised about the CEM differentiation timing data.

results.result: lin-29a is expressed in a male-specific, temporally controlled manner in 21 out of 116 sex-shared neuron classes. Expression begins at the L4 stage and is controlled by let-7-mediated regulation of lin-41, which directly represses lin-29a translation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance and were enthusiastic about the findings. The only comment related to Figure 3 was about labeling conventions, not the data itself.

results.result: lin-29a is both necessary and sufficient for the AIM neurotransmitter switch. Isoform-specific mutants fail to execute the switch, while ectopic expression causes premature switching and can induce the switch in hermaphrodites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers were very enthusiastic and recommended acceptance. No concerns were raised about the necessity and sufficiency experiments for lin-29a.

results.result: lin-29a controls multiple aspects of male-specific neuronal differentiation beyond the AIM neurotransmitter switch, including expression of srj-54 and dmd-5, daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons, and male-specific PDB neuron branching.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning these broader roles of lin-29a. The only comment about Figure 6C was a minor labeling issue, not about the data quality.

results.result: lin-29a mutants show defects in male mating behavior, including vulva location and mate searching. The mate searching defects can be partially rescued by restoring lin-29a expression specifically in AIM neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers were enthusiastic and recommended acceptance. No concerns were raised about the behavioral phenotypes or rescue experiments.

results.result: lin-29a mutants display feminization of body posture and locomotory features. These behavioral defects result from neuronal dysfunction rather than morphological changes, and can be partially rescued by expressing lin-29a in the motor circuit.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning the locomotory phenotype data or the circuit-specific rescue experiments.

results.result: The temporal, sexual, and spatial specificity of lin-29a expression is controlled intersectionally by the heterochronic pathway (lin-28/let-7/lin-41), the sex determination pathway (tra-1), and neuron-type-specific terminal selector transcription factors (unc-86, ttx-3, unc-3).
results.evaluation: Reviewers were very enthusiastic about the conceptual framework and recommended acceptance. No concerns were raised about the intersectional control mechanism.

results.result: mab-3 and dmd-3 are additional male-specific, neuron-type-specific targets of LIN-41 that are regulated by a similar intersectional mechanism involving the heterochronic pathway, sex determination pathway, and terminal selectors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance and were enthusiastic about the work. The extension to additional targets was not questioned. The only comment about Figure 9 was a minor reference error in the text.

results.result: mab-10 is not required for lin-29 function in AIM interneurons in males, despite functioning with lin-29 in seam cell differentiation and being a target of LIN-41.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning this negative result, which helps define the specificity of lin-29 cofactor requirements.

results.result: The timing of male-specific sexual maturation in the nervous system is independent of gonadal signals and the lin-4 miRNA, suggesting alternative pathways control lin-28 function timing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning these negative results, which help define the regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Expression analysis of lin-28, lin-41, and a let-7 activity sensor shows that these heterochronic pathway components are temporally controlled in the nervous system without sexual dimorphism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning the expression pattern data. These findings support the model of temporal control.

results.result: lin-29a mutant males do not display the morphological and patterning defects seen in lin-29 null mutants, with the male tail appearing normal and no overt morphological differences from wild-type males.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recommended acceptance without questioning these observations, which are important for interpreting the behavioral phenotypes as neuronal rather than morphological.

results.result: The regulation of lin-29 by terminal selectors like UNC-3 could potentially be direct, based on the presence of phylogenetically conserved UNC-3 binding sites in the lin-29 locus.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'It would have been nice to see the potential link between UNC-3 and lin-29 tested by removing the conserved binding sites to see if motor neuron expression is affected, but I would not suggest delaying publication for this experiment.' This indicates the claim is speculative and untested.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C36, C37, C49, C146. Both support the negative results for lin-4 and the positive results for glp-1 mutants. OpenEval notes these are unpublished observations ('data not shown'), slightly weakening reproducibility, but peer reviewers accepted without concern.

Perfect agreement on claims C99, C100, C101. Both support the distinction between lin-29a-specific and null phenotypes and the WormTracker morphological analysis. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on claims C109, C110, C111, C112. Both support the automated behavioral phenotyping and circuit-specific rescue experiments. OpenEval provides more detail on sample sizes (n=20) and specificity of effects.

Strong agreement on claims C88, C89, C90, C92, C96, C97, C98 regarding broad roles of lin-29a. Both evaluations support the findings. Peer review noted only minor figure labeling issues, not data quality concerns.

Strong agreement on claims C62, C63, C65, C66, C67, C68 regarding expression patterns and temporal control. Both support the use of multiple reporter types and appropriate controls. No concerns raised by peer reviewers.

Strong agreement on claims C121, C123-C129, C131, C133, C134 regarding mab-3 and dmd-3 regulation. Both support the extension of the intersectional control model to additional targets. Peer review noted only a minor text reference error.
Strong agreement on claims C102, C103, C105, C107 regarding behavioral phenotypes and rescue. Both support the findings with adequate sample sizes. No concerns raised by peer reviewers.

Strong agreement on claims C83, C84, C85, C86, C87 regarding lin-29a sufficiency experiments. Both support the cell autonomy, temporal sufficiency, and sex-specificity override demonstrations. Peer reviewers were very enthusiastic.
